claims.text: The homogenized cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy is initially single phase.
Aging HfNbTaTiZr at 600–800 °C induces nanoscale precipitates or early-stage phase segregation.
The aging-induced precipitates have a thermal expansion coefficient different from that of the matrix.
Thermal expansion mismatch between the matrix and precipitates generates residual stresses during cooling from the aging temperature.
The mismatch-induced residual stresses are localized near matrix–precipitate interfaces.
Residual thermal stresses alter dislocation mobility.
Residual thermal stresses alter lattice dynamics.
Mismatch-induced residual stresses provide a unified explanation for the alloy's creep, hardness, stress–strain, and thermoelastic behavior.
Relative to an as-homogenized control, aged samples will have improved creep resistance at 1250 °C.
The predicted improvement in creep resistance results from residual-stress-mediated impediment of dislocation motion.
Relative to the as-homogenized control, aged samples will have greater microhardness after cold rolling.
Relative to the as-homogenized control, aged samples will show a more pronounced temperature dependence of elastic moduli between 293 and 1100 K.
The as-homogenized baseline lacks the aging-induced precipitates and associated residual thermal stresses.
Comparing aged and unaged samples isolates the effect of precipitation-induced residual thermal stresses.
Rapid quenching can maintain the control specimens in an as-homogenized single-phase state.
X-ray or neutron diffraction can be used to assess residual stress levels associated with the proposed matrix–precipitate structure.
Earlier observations support the qualitative direction of the proposed effects.
A lack of statistically significant mechanical or thermoelastic differences between aged and unaged samples, or a lack of elevated residual stress in aged samples, would falsify the hypothesis.
